write.desc: This topic compares the sizes of infinite sets using bijections, shows that the natural numbers, integers, N x N and the rationals are all countable while infinite binary or decimal sequences are not, and so explains why the rationals are 'small' even though they are dense.

points.name: Same size: finite sets and bijections
points.what: The learner can define 'A has n elements' as a bijection with {1, ..., n} and 'A and B have the same cardinality' as the existence of a bijection between them, and can prove that having the same cardinality is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
outside: composition of functions and inverse functions

points.name: Countable sets: N, Z and the even numbers
points.what: The learner knows that 'countable' means finite or in bijection with N, can read a bijection with N as a list a1, a2, a3, ... with no repeats, and can write explicit bijections showing that the even numbers and the integers are countably infinite, so an infinite set can have the same size as a proper subset of itself.

points.name: Subsets of countable sets, injections and surjections
points.what: The learner can prove that every subset of a countable set is countable, by listing its elements in order, and can use the consequences: a set is countable if it injects into N, or if N maps onto it (or it is empty).
outside: well-ordering principle of the natural numbers

points.name: N x N is countable
points.what: The learner can show that the set of pairs of natural numbers is countable, both by the diagonal listing of the grid of pairs and by an explicit injection such as (m, n) -> 2^m 3^n, and can deduce that a finite product of countable sets is countable.

points.name: Countable unions of countable sets
points.what: The learner can prove that a union of countably many countable sets is countable by arranging the elements in a grid and mapping N x N onto the union, and can use the special cases that a union of two, or finitely many, countable sets is countable.
outside: indexed unions of a family of sets

points.name: The rationals are countable
points.what: The learner can give an explicit listing of the rationals (fractions p/q arranged in a grid, traversed diagonally and skipping repeats, then interleaving signs) and an injection-based proof, and understands that Q is countable even though there is a rational between any two numbers.

points.name: Cantor's diagonal argument for binary sequences
points.what: The learner can prove by contradiction that the set of infinite 0-1 sequences is uncountable: given any list of sequences, flipping the n-th digit of the n-th sequence produces a sequence missing from the list. The learner can reproduce this as a model proof.

points.name: Infinite decimals and why the reals should be uncountable
points.what: The learner can run the diagonal argument on infinite decimal expansions of numbers in (0, 1), choosing new digits that avoid 0 and 9 so that the double expansions such as 0.1999... = 0.2000... cause no trouble, and knows the rigorous proof that R is uncountable comes later from completeness.
outside: decimal expansions of numbers between 0 and 1

points.name: Countable versus uncountable: the irrationals and 'small' sets
points.what: The learner can deduce that the irrationals are uncountable because R would otherwise be a union of two countable sets, and understands that a countable set, however dense, is 'small' compared with an interval, an idea later used for discontinuities of monotone functions and for Thomae's function.

points.name: Comparing sizes with injections: Schroeder-Bernstein
points.what: The learner can read 'A is no bigger than B' as the existence of an injection from A into B, knows the Schroeder-Bernstein theorem (stated, not proved) that injections both ways give a bijection, and can use it to show, for example, that [0, 1] and (0, 1) have the same cardinality.

points.name: Cantor's theorem: no surjection onto the power set
points.what: The learner knows the power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A and can prove that no function from A onto P(A) exists by considering the set of elements not in their own image, so every set is strictly smaller than its power set and there is no largest infinite size.
